shared_text:
The flight. A wide-body airliner taking off much heavier than the crew usually flew. Daytime.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring. The captain had about 12,000 hours and the first officer about 4,500. Both had long experience on type but mostly flew lighter domestic flights. Because the captain had not flown an oceanic crossing for several years, preparation concentrated on oceanic procedures.

What happened. The departure had a 230-knot speed limit at a fix where it turned right; the clean manoeuvring speed was 261 knots. The briefing had not covered the limit, or keeping the slats out until after the turn. After a normal take-off and flap retraction, the captain called for slat retraction at about 240 knots, before the turn. The captain saw about 30 knots of margin above the minimum manoeuvring speed, with the aircraft accelerating. The first officer saw about 15–20 knots, and realised then that the crew had not considered the heavy weight with the 230-knot limit. The first officer paused, felt the captain look across, and retracted the slats, keeping a hand on the lever and judging the margin enough though smaller than normal. As the slats retracted the captain began the right turn, saw the minimum speed rising and reduced the bank, but it reached the airspeed and the stick shaker activated briefly. The first officer extended the slats at once, asking whether the captain wanted them out; the captain said, "I guess so."
safe_outcome: The slats stayed extended until the aircraft reached clean manoeuvring speed, and the rest of the departure was flown normally. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was climbing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
notes: Removed under rule 3: both reporters' later self-assessment ('multiple errors on my part', 'failed to brief', 'misjudged', 'Obviously I should have left them extended', 'no excuse', expectation bias and complacency, the PM's responsibility, the captain's comments on the company's overwater currency policy, and both summaries). Kept, as at-the-time or factual: the briefing gap is stated as an observable fact (both reporters agree); the first officer's realisation 'in that moment' is kept as a realisation at the time; each pilot's own reading of the speed margin (30 knots against 15–20 knots) is kept; the captain's reply is quoted. Moved under rule 5: slats kept out until clean manoeuvring speed and the rest of the departure. Cut for length: the first officer's late reassignment from relief first officer, and both pilots' 90-day hours. Removed under rule 6: departure, fix, runway and airport names; the redacted number of years on type is written as long experience on type. Judgement calls: the take-off weight figure (528.0) is left out because the report gives no unit; 'much heavier than the crew usually flew' is kept. The report's 'the foot' is written as the minimum manoeuvring speed on the speed tape. For James: this type is now flown almost only as a freighter, and the frozen bad ending mentions a flight attendant; the shared text says only 'wide-body airliner', so nothing contradicts it. Bracket 'climbing': the event is in the departure climb, where the natural conflict is another departing aircraft.
